summary: NFSv4 migration lets responsibility for a single file system move from one server to another without disrupting clients. Experience showed problems in how NFSv4.0 specified this. This proposed standard identifies those problem areas and gives revised specifications for them.

eli5.summary: Picture moving a library shelf to a new room while people are still borrowing books, without anyone noticing. This fixes the rules for doing that smoothly when a file server hands its files to another server.

subtitle: Fixes how NFSv4.0 servers hand a file system, and the locks on it, to another server without confusing clients.

tldr.problem: Implementation experience showed that the NFSv4.0 rules for moving a file system between servers left client state badly defined: rebooted clients kept stale state, servers ended up with several leases for one client, and clients had to juggle split locking state.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC replaces the client identity sections and the migration-and-state section of RFC 7530. It defines uniform and non-uniform client ID strings, says how migrated leases are merged with existing ones, and gives servers guidance for freezing lock state during a transfer.
tldr.outcome: It is a Standards Track update to RFC 7530, so it should be read together with that RFC by anyone implementing NFSv4.0 migration. It recommends the uniform client ID string approach for clients that want transparent state migration.

today: RFC 7931 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7530, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The sections it replaces in RFC 7530 are superseded by the text here.

sections.title: What This Update Corrects
sections.content:
RFC 7931 is a Standards Track document that corrects the definitive NFSv4.0 specification, RFC 7530. The RFC says readers should take it into account when learning NFSv4.0, especially for two topics: file system migration (particularly with transparent state migration) and the construction of the nfs_client_id4 structure, including the client ID string inside it.

Migration lets responsibility for a single file system move from one server to another without disrupting clients. The RFC works by replacing specific sections of RFC 7530 rather than rewriting the whole protocol: Sections 9.1.1 and 9.1.2 (client identity), Section 9.14 (migration, replication and state), Section 16.33 (SETCLIENTID), and part of the security considerations.
sections.eli5: The first rulebook for moving things between servers had some mistakes. This is the fix list, with the corrected rules.

sections.title: Problems Found in Practice
sections.content:
Implementers of transparent state migration found three symptoms. After a file system migrated, a reboot of the client was not handled well, because the state of the rebooting client was not promptly freed. A server could end up with multiple leases carrying the same nfs_client_id4, although the protocol assumes only one. And clients became complex, because one client could end up with its locking state on a given server split across several leases, each with its own clientid4.

The RFC concludes that the earlier specifications erred. They assumed locking state, including stateids and clientid4s, should be transferred, but never described how arriving state is merged into the client records that already exist on the destination server. The common client practice for presenting client ID strings made it nearly impossible for a client to tell whether two stateids from different servers belonged to the same client.

Clients trying an alternative approach also found that some servers did not work well with it, so the update has to untangle compatibility issues as well.
sections.eli5: When a shelf moved rooms, the new room sometimes wrote down the same person twice, and people had to carry several library cards. The fix is to make sure each person has one card, and the card follows them.

sections.title: How a Client Identifies Itself
sections.content:
NFSv4.0 uses three kinds of identity. The nfs_client_id4 structure holds a verifier and an opaque id string and identifies one client boot instance. The clientid4 is a shorthand value returned by the server after a successful SETCLIENTID and confirmed by SETCLIENTID_CONFIRM; it is tied to a lease. Owners of opens and byte-range locks are an opaque array plus a clientid4.

The verifier is a boot instance identifier. Only if it differs from the one the server recorded for that id does the server cancel the client's leased state, and only once the new record is confirmed. The server MUST NOT cancel state if the principal that established it differs from the one issuing the SETCLIENTID. Servers MUST NOT reject an id merely because it is not valid UTF-8.

The client ID string should be unique, should stay the same across reboots, and should not assume the client's network address stays fixed. The RFC lists ways a clientid4 becomes invalid: server reboot, a wrong id sent, lease expiry, a suspected client reboot, administrative revocation, and two migration cases (all state migrated away, or a lease merged into another). Reboot-like cases destroy the clientid4 and all stateids; migration cases destroy only the clientid4 while stateids stay valid.
sections.eli5: A client shows a name tag (the id string) and a boot sticker (the verifier). The server hands back a short number to use afterwards, like a library card number.

sections.title: Uniform and Non-uniform Client ID Strings
sections.content:
The RFC names two valid approaches. With the non-uniform approach the client presents different id strings to different server addresses, so each address sees a separate client. This is NFSv3-like and keeps clients simple, but the RFC says clients supporting migration with transparent state migration are likely to have difficulties with it, because a migrated lease can leave several leases for the same client on one server.

With the uniform approach the client presents the same id string everywhere. The server can then keep a single lease per client and merge leases automatically during migration, with no client involvement. For that reason the RFC recommends the uniform approach for clients supporting transparent state migration. The verifier should change if and only if a new client instance is created, so it should be established once per reboot.

The uniform approach has costs: it differs from what most clients do today, mapping server addresses to leases is no longer one-to-one, and it lets cooperating servers see that requests come from the same client, which is a privacy concern. Some existing servers also misbehave with it, for example by returning NFS4ERR_CLID_INUSE just because the same client has a clientid4 from another address. A client can therefore use different approaches for different mounts, typically chosen by mount options.
sections.eli5: Either you give every shop a different name tag, or you wear the same one everywhere. The same name tag lets the shops that share a back room notice you are one person, which helps when things move.

sections.title: Working Out Which Addresses Are One Server
sections.content:
NFSv4.0 does not say whether two server IP addresses reach the same server. A client using the uniform approach can infer it, and the RFC gives an example procedure (clients need not follow it exactly). The same clientid4 from two addresses is necessary but not sufficient to conclude they are the same server. Servers MUST NOT give a client two different clientid4s yet treat them as one client.

In the example, the client does SETCLIENTID to a new address X and gets a clientid4 and confirm value. If no known address has that clientid4, X is a new server and the client confirms. If it matches, the client sends a SETCLIENTID to each matching lead address to get a fresh confirm value, then tries each of those values in a SETCLIENTID_CONFIRM sent to X. If one is accepted, X and that address are the same server. If none is accepted, X is a distinct server. At most one confirm should succeed.

The RFC also covers racing lookups (serialize them in one of three ways of increasing parallelism), server reboots during the procedure (use RENEW to check), and what to do when a probe takes too long to answer.
sections.eli5: To find out whether two doors lead to the same shop, you hand a note through one door and see if the other door recognizes it.

sections.title: Moving State Along With the File System
sections.content:
Servers involved in a migration should transfer all state for the file system to the destination, and if they do, the transfer MUST be transparent to the client. The client keeps using the stateids it already has, and the new server must treat them as the same locks (same file, lock type, particulars and owner strings). If moving stateids would conflict with an existing stateid for that client, transparent migration MUST NOT happen for that client. A client can check the outcome by using a stateid on the new server: NFS4ERR_BAD_STATEID means no transparent migration (or the state was purged on a verifier mismatch), while a valid stateid means it worked.

If a server chooses not to transfer state, which is discouraged, it MUST provide a file-system-specific grace period so clients can reclaim locks. For clientid4s, an existing lease with the same id string and verifier SHOULD be merged with the migrated one, with the latest renewal winning. If only the id string matches, the server MUST eliminate one of the two. The destination may substitute a different clientid4 if the transferred one is already in use.

Owner information (the last sequence number and the result of the last operation) SHOULD move with the state for owners used only on that file system; owners spanning several file systems need the more careful rules in the RFC, such as keeping the greater sequence value when merging. Replication is different: leases, stateids and client IDs have no validity across servers, and the client must re-establish locks.
sections.eli5: When the shelf moves, the list of who borrowed what moves with it. If the two rooms would end up with clashing cards, the move is called off for that person.

sections.title: Telling Clients the Lease Moved
sections.content:
A client may not touch a moved file system for a while, so the server reports the move when leases are renewed. Operations that implicitly renew leases (OPEN, CLOSE, READ, WRITE, RENEW, LOCK and others) return NFS4ERR_LEASE_MOVED if responsibility for any lease being renewed has moved. The lease is still renewed when state remains on the source server.

A client that supports migration MUST then do a GETATTR of the fs_locations attribute for each migrated file system holding its state, which proves to the server that it knows about the move. By convention these compounds SHOULD include an appended RENEW. After that the server MUST resume normal handling of stateful requests. For legacy clients, the server SHOULD time out after at least two lease periods; later accesses get NFS4ERR_MOVED.

The lease_time attribute on the destination must never be less than on the source. If state was not transferred, the client should fetch the new server's value, and the new server must respect a grace period at least as long as the source's lease_time.
sections.eli5: The librarian tells you the shelf moved next time you check in, and you must go and look at the sign showing the new room before you can borrow again.

sections.title: Guidance for Server Implementers
sections.content:
Servers must stop locking state from changing while it is copied, or the destination would differ from what the client expects. A server can return NFS4ERR_DELAY for operations that would change state, but two problems arise: owner sequence values still change even when NFS4ERR_DELAY is returned, and some operations (OPEN_CONFIRM, RELEASE_LOCKOWNER and RENEW) were not allowed to return it.

Returning NFS4ERR_DELAY on a PUTFH into the target file system, or on a LOOKUP or LOOKUPP that crosses into it, handles most of this. The RFC distinguishes a time T, after which those operations return NFS4ERR_DELAY, from a later time T' when state is considered fixed. RENEW is handled by giving the destination lease an expiry no earlier than the latest renewal, and RELEASE_LOCKOWNER either by forwarding the deletion or by returning NFS4ERR_DELAY.

The RFC therefore allows RELEASE_LOCKOWNER to return NFS4ERR_DELAY, but only to clients prepared for file system migration, and the source server MUST NOT do so unless it is likely to return NFS4ERR_MOVED later. A layered approach with a preparatory phase and a restrictive phase limits how long the broad delay lasts. It also redefines NFS4ERR_CLID_INUSE and revises SETCLIENTID processing.
sections.eli5: Before moving the list of borrowers, the librarian asks everyone to wait a moment, so the list does not change while it is being copied.
